body_markdown:
“I don’t think I’ve driven one of those since high school,” I say, staring at the impeccable red XJ Cherokee. Memories from 30 years ago flood my brain; suddenly I’m in Northern Virginia, headed to 7-Eleven for a Slurpee after cross-country practice and making all sorts of questionable decisions with my buddies in their XJs. I grin without realizing it.


Fellow editor Kyle Smith is the consummate enabler. “Let’s fix that,” he says. I snap back into the present to catch the keys he tosses me.


I thumb the door handle’s release button. Its familiar click and the swing of the featherweight door welcome me as if I were opening the screen door of my childhood home. I climb into the two-door XJ’s cabin; it’s all so familiar. The airy view with low sills and thin pillars. The boxy dash and trim and that spindly pre-airbag wheel. Those fat needles for the tach and speedo. And ** that plastic-and-cloth Chrysler smell to top it all off; few cars are such a time warp for me, but that’s probably because there were at least 15 of them in my high-school parking lot.


Jordan Lewis


Yes, the XJ Cherokee is now well and truly one of those collector vehicles that people of a certain age fondly look back on and use to harness memories. That said, from its very successful inception in 1983 until now, the XJ has *always* had a strong following and has been enthusiastically put to use, whether as a first car, an off-roader, or anything in between. (For an excellent history lesson on the XJ’s international roots, check out Jason Cammisa’s *Revelations* story[here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3L7vlWUndU) .) I figured my chance meeting with Hagerty’s 1993 example a month ago up in Traverse City, Michigan, was as good a moment as any to remind myself of what makes the XJ continue to be a compelling everyday ride as well as a sought-after emerging collector vehicle.


The 4.0-liter High Output straight-six cranks to life and settles into a healthy thrum. I slot the long-handled shifter into first and trundle out of the Hagerty garage just by slowly releasing the clutch. A few blocks down the road, the Cherokee feels like the automotive version of an old, broken-in baseball glove: It’s not a precision fit, but it’s quickly become an extension of my body.


[Jordan Lewis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/jlewishagerty-com/)


The latter bit is usually a description reserved for sports cars, and it certainly wouldn’t work for any of today’s hefty SUVs. It’s apt in this instance, though; the XJ is surprisingly light on its feet and responsive to inputs. The engine’s healthy torque pairs with a short set of gears (even in the automatics, if my memory serves) to make the H.O.-powered Cherokee always feel eager, if not truly quick. The steering, brakes, and shifter might not yield exacting detail, but their low-effort nature and the XJ’s lack of mass (under 3000 pounds) combine for a surprisingly engaging drive. Those thin doors and big greenhouse offer no-fat simplicity in stark contrast to insular modern transportation. I pull back into the shop after a 10-or-so-mile loop, bright-eyed from the rekindled experiences and genuinely impressed at what[AMC and Renault created](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/remembering-vince-geraci-stalwart-of-amc-design/) more than 40 years ago, and what Chrysler and Jeep wisely kept alive.


Jordan Lewis


Jordan Lewis


Kyle made my evening by sharing the Jeep’s keys, but he’s not the only XJ fan in the Hagerty Media bullpen. Brandan Gillogly has owned a ’98 four-door automatic for almost seven years and still loves it. “One of the best things about owning an XJ is that at this point, you’ll never be the first one to have that particular issue,” he says. “There are always forum posts or YouTube videos on how to do all the major fixes.” The problem points are well known—check out[our buyer’s guide](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1984-2001-jeep-cherokee-xj-buyers-guide/) to learn about them as well as the XJ’s evolution over its production. Even though it had 135,000 miles on it when he bought it, Brandan reports that he’s just had to perform basic maintenance along with front hubs, a water pump, and a cam position sensor. “That last one is notoriously a pain,” he says. “I got a pretty good deal when I bought it, and it’s probably the only vehicle I’ve ever owned that has actually maintained its value.”


Jordan Lewis


The good news for folks who are interested in an XJ is that even though they’ve begun to transition into collector status, they’re not yet expensive, especially for driver-quality examples. The absolute best, new-in-wrapper XJs (there aren’t many of these left) can get into the mid-$30K range, while excellent examples can be found in the lower $20s. Driver-condition cars—the ones that make up the meat of the market—can be had for anywhere between eight and 15 grand. While the two-door is considerably rarer, at only 14% of the market, it doesn’t command a meaningful premium over the four-doors. Likewise, there’s no premium for manual-equipped Cherokees—that’s because they were typically found on lower trims and as such the value of the options tend to offset that of the transmission.


Appreciation for the Cherokee appears to be near-universal. The generations that knew the XJ when it was still rolling out of its Toledo, Ohio, assembly plant hold the most policies, with boomers at 40%, Gen X at 33%, and millennials at 18%. Younger enthusiasts are seeking a lot of quotes, though, with millennials making up 29% of inquiries and Gen Z coming in at 14%, suggesting that the XJ is going to remain a popular choice for years to come. I’m glad for that; it’s a perfect old-car recipe of memory-making, practicality, and fun.


Jordan Lewis
